title: UK to review Chagos Islands deal over lack of US support, Streeting tells BBC
description: The UK is reviewing its deal to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, the defence secretary has said.Wes Streeting confirmed the deal was being l
body: The UK is reviewing its deal to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, the defence secretary has said.Wes Streeting confirmed the deal was being looked at again after US President Donald Trump called it "terrible" at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday.The original agreement would see the UK cede sovereignty of the territory to Mauritius and pay an average of £101m ($136m) per year to lease back a joint UK-US military base there, prized for its strategic location in the Indian Ocean.In April the deal, agreed under Sir Keir Starmer, was paused indefinitely because Trump pulled his support.Streeting said "we have to" review the deal "because the United States doesn't support it"."What President Trump said yesterday wasn't new but I think it does provide absolute clarity that his position on this Chagos deal as currently drafted is not changing," he told BBC Breakfast."So we have to do more work with our American allies, with President Trump and his administration, to get the deal to a place where he can support it."Streeting said the focus now would be to secure a long-term certainty for the base on Diego Garcia, the Chagos archipelago's largest island.He said it had been the view of every UK prime minister since Boris Johnson that an ongoing legal process - as Mauritius argues it was illegally forced to give away the islands in 1965 to gain independence - risks the security of the base.During Trump's first face-to-face meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the UN General Assembly in New York, the US president criticised the "terrible deal" and said the UK was "going to be looking" at it.Burnham replied: "Yep."He later told broadcasters he has "inherited the situation and we need a resolution".Burnham added: "It's critical to safeguard the future of the base, and that matters to us for security reasons, but also clearly to the United States as well."What I said in the meeting is that we will work to find that resolution between the different sides, and we'll work hard to find it."The prime minister had spoken to his Mauritian counterpart, Navin Ramgoolam, ahead of his trip to New York, and an official readout from that meeting said Burnham "reiterated his commitment to continue doing everything possible" along with the US to ratify the deal.The "review" is not expected to constitute a formal process operating to a specific timeframe.Government sources are insisting that Burnham and Streeting's comments do not represent a major shift from the previous position, which was that any deal would require American support.However Streeting's comments were notable for their explicit acknowledgement that without changes the deal is not going to attract Trump's support.Prior to the pause in April, the UK and Mauritius had signed an agreement in May 2025 and a final draft of the bill to hand over sovereignty of the islands had not passed Parliament.Under the terms of the deal agreed in 2025, Britain would hand sovereignty over the archipelago to Mauritius but lease back the Diego Garcia base for 99 years, which the UK government said would be a net overall cost of £3.4bn.However, Sir Keir, who was then prime minister, came under heavy criticism from opponents who said the real cost of the deal could amount to £35bn, adjusting for inflation, and risked allowing China to establish a presence on the archipelago.Trump, who originally backed the deal, has been a frequent critic of the move, previously branding it a "a blight on our great ally" and an "act of total weakness".Reacting to the review, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch called on Burnham to "just scrap this terrible deal".Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said: "The Chagos deal is dead. Thank God."In 2019, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) gave an advisory opinion that Britain's separation of the Chagos Islands from Mauritius was unlawful and stated the UK must end its administration as rapidly as possible.While non-binding, the ICJ advisory opinion - which was endorsed by the United Nations General Assembly - emboldened Mauritian assertions of sovereignty and led to the UK opening negotiations in 2022.Streeting told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Wednesday that no money would be handed over to Mauritius "at this stage" while officials review the deal.Describing the Diego Garcia base as "one of the most sensitive and valuable national security assets", he said work was underway to find a deal "that maybe not everyone loves, but everyone can live with".

schema.headline: UK to review Chagos Islands deal over lack of US support, Streeting tells BBC

title: Gary Anderson: On-the-run killer arrested in Donegal
description: A man who was convicted of murder and has been unlawfully at large for over a week has been arrested in the Republic of Ireland.Gary Anderson, 29, was
body: A man who was convicted of murder and has been unlawfully at large for over a week has been arrested in the Republic of Ireland.Gary Anderson, 29, was jailed for life in 2023, alongside his brother, for the murder of Karol Kelly in Londonderry.He was on temporary release from prison to attend his father's funeral when he absconded.He was arrested on Wednesday by An Garda Síochána (Irish police) at a property in the town of Buncrana in County Donegal.Karol Kelly's sister said her family felt "let down" by the justice system.The Justice Minister, Naomi Long, is due to meet the family later this week.Anderson failed to return to prison on 14 September and was last seen in the Eastway area of Derry.Det Insp Gareth Lavery of the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) thanked "everyone who assisted with our enquiries since our public appeal last Monday". He added that officers "conducted extensive enquiries during this investigation to locate Gary Anderson".Lavery also thanked An Garda Síochána officers "who arrested Gary Anderson today and for all of their help with this investigation over the last week"."PSNI is now working with relevant authorities in order to return Gary Anderson to custody, and we will provide an update in due course." An Garda Síochána asid they arrested a man, aged in his 20s, in Donegal as "part of a planned operation"."He is being detained under the provisions of Section 4 of the Criminal Justice Act, 1984, at a station in the Garda North Western Region."Buncrana is about a 30-minute drive from the Irish border.The town is popular with visitors from the north-west of Northern Ireland.

schema.headline: Gary Anderson: On-the-run killer arrested in Donegal

title: Netanyahu calls Macron's West Bank comments in UN speech 'grotesque'
description: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has condemned French President Emmanuel Macron after he criticised Israel's actions in the occupied West Ban
body: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has condemned French President Emmanuel Macron after he criticised Israel's actions in the occupied West Bank during his address to the UN General Assembly."Look at what's happening in the West Bank, where day in, day out, we are seeing violations. And in the name of what? Hamas was never very active in the West Bank," Macron said in French, according to the UN's interpreter.Netanyahu called the remarks a "grotesque absurdity" and said members of the Palestinian armed group there "carry out attacks against Jews almost every day".There was no response from Macron's office, but one French diplomatic source said there had been a "misinterpretation".The source told the Jerusalem Post, external that the meaning of the French sentence spoken by the president, "Le Hamas n'a jamais sévi en Cisjordanie," was, "Hamas has never governed the West Bank." Macron also rejected US President Donald Trump's assertion that he had ended the war between Israel and Hamas in the Gaza Strip. Violence there has continued despite last October's ceasefire, including almost daily Israeli strikes, while humanitarian conditions remain dire"Some boast of a supposed peace. But that peace has not reopened humanitarian access for a single second," he said. "Are we simply to stand by and watch this spectacle that should shame us all?"After the address, the Israeli prime minister's office said in a statement: "The grotesque absurdity of Emmanuel Macron's statement is staggering.""On Sunday, the eve of [the Jewish holy day of] Yom Kippur, just two days ago, Netanel Shukrun - a French citizen and father of six - was murdered in his car by a Hamas terrorist in Judea and Samaria," it added, using a biblical term for the West Bank."Hamas terrorists carry out attacks against Jews almost every day. They have murdered countless Israeli civilians in Judea and Samaria."The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, also denounced Macron's remarks as "out of touch with reality".Shukrun, 36, was shot dead when a Palestinian opened fire on a group of Israelis at a spring near the West Bank settlement of Neve Tzuf, according to Israeli police. The suspect was arrested later at a hospital in the city of Ramallah, they said.Hamas praised the attack but did not say it was behind it.The group - which is designated as a terrorist organisation by Israel, France and other countries - is a rival of the Fatah-dominated Palestinian Authority, which governs parts of the West Bank that are not under Israeli control.Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem - land Palestinians want, along with Gaza, for a hoped-for future state - during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.The settlements are illegal under international law.

schema.headline: Netanyahu calls Macron's West Bank comments in UN speech 'grotesque'

title: England players carrying 'scar' from World Cup exit, says Bukayo Saka
description: England winger Bukayo Saka says the team are still carrying the "scar" of their heartbreaking World Cup semi-final exit to Argentina.Thomas Tuchel's t
body: England winger Bukayo Saka says the team are still carrying the "scar" of their heartbreaking World Cup semi-final exit to Argentina.Thomas Tuchel's team were on the verge of becoming the first England side to reach a men's World Cup final since 1966, but were stunned by two late Argentina goals as they fell to a 2-1 loss.A thrilling 6-4 victory over France in the bronze medal match gave the Three Lions their best World Cup finish in six decades, but the wait for their second trophy goes on."Obviously, there is still a scar on us when you believed and everyone was so united and so confident we could do it," Saka said."Not just us, but the whole country we felt."You try to move on as soon as possible, but you know a scar is a scar, it decides to heal when it heals itself."England get an immediate reminder of what might have been as they host world champions Spain at Wembley on Saturday (19:45 BST) in the first of four Nations League matches over the next two weeks."We are trying to draw a line under [the World Cup] now and focus on the new international season that we have coming up," Saka added."We have got four massive, difficult group games to try and qualify us for the Nations League [knockouts] that we are really focused on."Meanwhile, Saka believes it is only a matter of time before his Arsenal team-mate Max Dowman, 16, earns a senior England call-up."I think so," Saka said. "His talent is insane. It's up to him how far he is going to go in football. His talent is crazy."England Under-21 manager Lee Carsley concurred with Saka on Dowman's "amazing talent" but thinks the youngster staying with the under-19s during this international window is the best option."He is more than capable of playing in the under-21s," Carsley said."What I do think will happen with the age group he goes to is that he can play the minutes."He can also have that time to consolidate where he is in his career and play with his friends again and take that little bit of pressure off him."I have no doubt that Max is going to be with the under-21s."That is something I am keen to have a conversation with him and his parents, on the way we see his pathway going, because he is an amazing talent and someone we are very lucky to have."

schema.headline: England players carrying 'scar' from World Cup exit, says Bukayo Saka

title: Admiral UK insurance to cut 500 jobs to save £100m
description: Insurer Admiral will cut 500 jobs in the UK to save £100m, it has announced.The proposals are related to Admiral's UK insurance business only, and wil
body: Insurer Admiral will cut 500 jobs in the UK to save £100m, it has announced.The proposals are related to Admiral's UK insurance business only, and will affect about 5% of its workforce."We recognise this will be a difficult time for affected colleagues," said Alistair Hargreaves, Admiral Insurance UK's chief executive .While the Cardiff-based company uses artificial intelligence (AI) in its operations, adoption of AI is not believed to be responsible for these changes.Admiral said the job cuts would make the firm "faster and more efficient".Earlier this year, Admiral said it needed to save £100m, and has added the proposed redundancies are part of that cost-cutting effort."These changes are aimed at making us faster and more efficient so we can continue to deliver great customer outcomes," said Hargreaves.Staff members who are affected will be offered "enhanced" redundancy payments and redeployment opportunities where possible.Hargreaves said Admiral was also "making a significant investment in meaningful support to help colleagues consider future options".

schema.headline: Admiral UK insurance to cut 500 jobs to save £100m

title: Thélyson Orélien: French uproar over author accused of using AI
description: The French book scene is in uproar after a Canadian-Haitian author billed as a sensation was accused of using artificial intelligence (AI) to write hi
body: The French book scene is in uproar after a Canadian-Haitian author billed as a sensation was accused of using artificial intelligence (AI) to write his first novel.Thélyson Orélien, 38, has just been awarded the Prix du Roman Fnac – the first of the literary season's prizes – for C'était ça ou mourir (It was either that or die).  He is also a finalist for the most prestigious annual French language awards, the Goncourt and the Renaudot, set to be issued soon.But on Tuesday a little-known group called Balance ton Claude (Denounce your Claude, in reference to Anthropic's AI assistant) claimed the book was "almost totally" written by AI - a charge the author denied."We tested several passages, from different bits of the manuscript, to come up with the identical result: 100 percent AI," the group said on X.According to the group – whose membership is unclear – the detection was carried out by a programme called Pangram, which it said was "by far the most accurate", with an almost negligible chance of making a mistake.Orélien, who was born in Haiti and moved to Montreal in 2010, immediately denied the accusation."I have always loved creation and literature. I can't see why I would feel compelled to use a machine," he told Libération newspaper. He said he was "compiling a dossier" with his editor to prove that he authentically wrote the book."My traditions are Haitian and Caribbean. The images, the repetitions and the rhythms are the living word, they are my own," he said.The publishing house Grasset also came to his defence, saying the allegations "are atrociously injurious to a writer with an exceptional life-story" whose "work of creation is original and powerful."The novel tells the story of a teacher who flees gang violence in Haiti and his adventures before he finally makes it to Canada, where he re-discovers "the right to breathe without fear".The row recalls the controversy over Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir's The Serpent in the Grove, whose Commonwealth Short Story prize was initially withdrawn in July over allegations that it was written with generative AI.The prize was subsequently re-awarded, after the organisers said they were satisfied the writing was genuine.Critics of Pangram and other AI-detectors say they are unreliable – with different programmes often giving different results after analysing the same texts.These tools do not actually know who, or what, wrote a piece of text. Instead, they look for patterns commonly found in AI-generated writing, but those patterns can also appear in human work.Research has found that AI-detectors can wrongly flag human writing as AI-generated and miss text that was produced by artificial intelligence, particularly if it has been edited or paraphrased.Some also say that the programmes are built around the use of standardised language - English or French - and so cannot accurately interpret texts that use dialect from places like the Caribbean.But the writers behind Balance ton Claude said that Pangram had been shown to make a wrong call about an AI-generated text only one time in every 24,400.The latest detectors no longer compare text with text, to see if there has been plagiarism. Instead they analyse probabilities and statistics, to see if certain linguistic patterns betray the use of AI.With AI becoming increasingly normalised, the row over C'etait ça ou mourir will feed the debate over what mix of human and AI creativity is deemed acceptable – it being perfectly possible for writers to generate AI then adapt it, or conversely write an original text then ask AI to review it.Orélien was born in 1988 in the northern Haitian city of Gonaives.  His first work – before leaving his homeland – consisted of mainly poetic texts, and later in Canada he worked as a journalist.   The novel, described by his Canadian publisher as its biggest seller in 60 years, is due to be translated into around 20 languages.Orélien told Libération that the first draft of the book was written in 2019 – well before AI programmes to generate text became generally available.

schema.headline: Thélyson Orélien: French uproar over author accused of using AI

title: Advert break during Arsenal Champions League game was unscheduled
description: A three-minute advert break during a Women's Champions League game was not scheduled, Disney+ confirmed.Arsenal and HB Koge were drawing 0-0 in the se
body: A three-minute advert break during a Women's Champions League game was not scheduled, Disney+ confirmed.Arsenal and HB Koge were drawing 0-0 in the second half on Tuesday when coverage was interrupted.It was one of several technical issues during the coverage, which fans said was "gimmicky" and "undermines" women's football. One guest was a dog with 137,000 Instagram followers.Disney confirmed it was an unintended interruption caused by a technical issue and understood the frustration caused. It was making steps to ensure it did not happen again.Arsenal won 1-0 in their first game of this season's competition thanks to a stoppage-time Mariona Caldentey penalty.Disney's coverage also featured a vegetable platter being served and a rotating floor.Alex Scott hosted the first show of the season, alongside former England forward Lianne Sanderson, content creators Alex Bailess and Tyra Mills, and a dog called Barley Boy.There was no explanation for his presence on set other than his Instagram following.It was the second season of the Women's Champions League to be broadcast on Disney+. Matches are produced by ESPN.New this season is "The Hangout", described by Disney as a live studio show billed as a "new match-day experience for fans, delivering pre-match build-up, half-time analysis and post-match reaction".In a media release before the first round of fixtures, Disney said: "The Hangout will combine expert analysis with fresh perspectives and fan engagement."However, the evening was marred by a series of technical issues – from players waiting to be interviewed but unable to hear questions from the studio, to a rotating floor that appeared to have a mind of its own.There were also camera shots with cushions blocking the view of Scott, and audio synchronisation problems.Italian reporter Roberto Perrone, in Milan for Inter Milan's match against Swedish side Hacken, also encountered audio problems.When the sound returned, viewers were shown a non-football-themed quiz, with questions ranging from types of pasta to Italy's biggest city.One fan wrote on X: "I think a lot of the problem with the debates in women's football broadcasting over analysis and punditry vs content creation and gimmicky fun, is that in men's football you can get both - and in different shows."In women's football, you get one show, and so they try to do it all."Another fan wrote: "We want women's football to be taken seriously, yet coverage like this undermines that. Personality and fun have their place, but not at the expense of the football."The game doesn't need gimmicks to make it interesting. Give the players, the competition and the football itself the same focus, analysis and respect we expect elsewhere in the sport. "Women's football is more than capable of being the main event."Megan Feringa, a journalist for the Athletic, said: "Watching Disney's coverage is like going in and out of a lucid dream."Why is there a dog? Why is the couch spinning? Why do the adverts cut right into analysis?"Flo Lloyd-Hughes, a broadcaster and writer for the Cutback, said: "Why does women's football coverage always have to be so gimmicky? It's the Champions League, not Blue Peter. "Put some pundits who know about the teams in a studio, make sure the tech works and have a decent bit of time for build-up and analysis to contextualise everything."Last November concerns were raised over the professionalism and legitimacy of the Women's League Cup quarter-final and semi-final draw, which was conducted by social media influencer GK Barry. In the same month Sky Sports scrapped its new female-focused TikTok channel, Halo, after it faced a backlash online, with its posts described as "patronising" and "sexist".Disney+ coverage continues on Wednesday with Chelsea hosting Austria Wien at 20:00 BST.

schema.headline: Advert break during Arsenal Champions League game was unscheduled

title: Open wounds and eyes that can't close - women warn about cheap bleph eyelid surgery
description: They have told the BBC the demand for this procedure, which normally costs thousands of pounds in the UK, has increased as part of a wider aesthetic t
body: They have told the BBC the demand for this procedure, which normally costs thousands of pounds in the UK, has increased as part of a wider aesthetic trend to tighten, smooth and lift the face.Surgeons say complications have been linked to clinics across mainland Europe, Africa and Asia, and, when they occur, the lack of aftercare puts a burden on the NHS.As well as Nikita, we have spoken to dozens of people who have experienced problems - including one woman who had to tape her eyes shut to sleep because too much eyelid skin had been removed, while another feared she was losing her sight. UK surgeons have also told us they have seen patients unable to close their eyes properly after treatment abroad. Nikita, from Dublin, wanted to make her eyes more defined, but could not afford upper eyelid surgery in Ireland that she was told would cost more than €4,000 (£3,400).Then the 31-year-old discovered on TikTok that she could get a bleph with Dutch company, Faceland for €750 (£650).She described its clinic in Düsseldorf as "like a conveyor belt, just one in, one out constantly".The company says it has performed more than 2,950 bleph procedures on UK patients at its clinics in the Netherlands, Germany and Switzerland since October 2024.It says it offers "safe and quality" treatments and told us "less than 1% of procedures have led to a complaint", although this does not include everyone who needed revision surgery.The majority of patients who spoke to the BBC about problems with their blephs had been to the company's clinics - but we do not know how many complications in total have occurred at Faceland.Nikita, who went for her bleph in November 2025, says she did not realise how invasive the procedure would be, believing it to be like "getting your lips or Botox done", she says.She was injected with local anaesthetic, but when the doctor began cutting delicate eyelid skin, she felt pain she had never experienced before."I went into shell shock, it was horrible," Nikita says. "When she was stitching me I could feel the needle going through my skin."In the past three years, videos about blephs posted by UK social media accounts on four leading platforms were viewed nearly 150 million times, BBC analysis has found. This figure is five times greater than the previous three years.Many people report positive results in their posts, and a lot have been treated at Faceland.One woman told us her droopy eyelids had been restricting her vision and causing her headaches. She was not eligible for NHS treatment and could not afford to go private in the UK, but now she says, after going to Faceland, her issues have been resolved.The company's website claims it is changing the market by focusing on "affordable, accessible and high quality care". Treatments are carried out by accredited medical doctors who receive internal training by Faceland in surgical procedures, it says.Surgeons in the UK told us upper eyelid surgery typically takes about three hours, including preparation, surgery and post-operation care. But Faceland patients we have spoken to say they spent less than an hour at the clinics.Faceland says allowing practitioners to perform a higher volume of treatments helps significantly lower costs.Eight days after her Faceland bleph surgery, Laura, not her real name, made her first of four visits to A&E because her eyelid wounds had reopened.Her procedure at the company's Amsterdam clinic in June had seemingly gone smoothly, but problems began when she took her stitches out back home in the UK, something many patients do when they have treatment abroad.The crescent shaped cuts above her eyes which had been held together by the stitches came apart, exposing raw, red wounds which became infected. This should hardly ever happen if a practitioner has been properly trained, UK surgeons told us.The first time this happened, Laura, who is in her early 40s, says she called Faceland's emergency helpline several times, but could not get through. Desperate, she rushed to A&E."When I closed my eyes for too long the tension would cause my wounds to open up again," she says. "I was scared to go to sleep and was in constant agony."The BBC has seen emails that show Caryn contacted Faceland twice, to report what had happened, and that she received a short reply 12 days later. A few further emails followed, but Caryn says she has not heard from the company since.Faceland maintains it "did not leave her without support or follow-up during the aftercare process".It says it is sorry if patients felt insufficiently supported by its teams or experienced complications.Like Caryn, Laura and Nikita, patients we have spoken to who have had cheap eyelid surgery abroad say limited aftercare is their biggest complaint."Aftercare for the typical bleph should be available to a patient 24/7," says Vize. "If your surgeon is hundreds of miles away, the ability to provide care with a sense of immediacy is impossible."He also warns that patients should be aware that in some cases lower costs may mean lower standards.The company also says patients can come back to a Faceland clinic to have stitches removed, but no-one we spoke to had done that.Patients removing their own stitches is "a recipe for disaster", according to Vize, who says stitches should be taken out by a surgeon or a nurse to reduce the infection risk and the chance of wounds splitting open.Nikita is mostly happy with her results, aside from a small scar, but she wants other people to learn from her experiences and fully understand the risks."If I'd had the money or if I hadn't listened to the spin on TikTok, I probably would have gone somewhere closer to home and not rushed into it," she says.Nearly two years on, Caryn still has issues with her left eye, including some blurry vision and scarring.Meanwhile, Laura fears she may have scars above both of her eyes for life."I tried to fix a problem that didn't really need fixing, and I've come back with a bigger problem that I need surgery for, and I can't afford that," she says. "It's pretty devastating."

schema.headline: Open wounds and eyes that can't close - women warn about cheap bleph eyelid surgery

title: England vs Sri Lanka: Will Jacks explains the "scary" detail behind emergency appendix surgery
description: Jacks was given an initial four-week recovery period but ended up returning a few days early to captain the Lions in a warm-up against Sri Lanka on 11
body: Jacks was given an initial four-week recovery period but ended up returning a few days early to captain the Lions in a warm-up against Sri Lanka on 11 September.Afterwards he played in all three T20s in England's series sweep against the same opponents, and on Tuesday took career-best 50-over figures of 5-22 in the first one-day international in Chester-le-Street."Luckily they were able to do a slight incision and not have to rip me open completely," he said.Appendix operations are not rare but they do not fit naturally with the twisting and turning of a spin bowler's action, meaning Jacks has been doing extra work behind the scenes to rebuild his core strength.It makes the 4.3 degrees of turn Jacks found at Chester-le-Street – the most he has produced at home in his ODI career – even more impressive, albeit helped by a slow pitch.His figures were also the second best by an England spinner in one-day internationals."It was more of a confidence thing," he said."It helped that we were playing the T20s first and I was bowling a maximum of four overs."If I am honest, I only bowled five days before the first game because I was building up my strength and trying to get some fitness back."I didn't bowl too much in the T20 series, which probably benefited me. It has been OK."Jacks' match in the north east also included an important 46 not out with the bat.Though he was eventually left stranded, he batted responsibly, hitting only one four in his first 43 deliveries, to make sure England's innings was extended from 211-7 in the 39th over to 265 in the penultimate."I came in and found it really difficult to start off," he said."I just re-evaluated what I thought was a good score and obviously what then happened with wickets falling around me a change of the role, just try and bat out the overs."For so long "batting out the overs" has not been the England way, but Jacks is a player growing in maturity.He is also vice-captain to Harry Brook for these Sri Lanka series in the absence of Jacob Bethell and has become an increasingly vocal member of the group.It was telling that when England's T20 World Cup campaign began earlier this year amid the cloud of Brook's Wellington episode, Jacks was first put up to speak to the media."He's just a good leader," Brook said, plainly.Reliable off the field, Jacks is becoming increasingly so on it.It is 18 months since he moved from the top of the order to the middle as England's finisher in T20 and 50-over cricket. After obvious success as England's player of the tournament at the T20 World Cup in India and Sri Lanka, this was another sign of his growing confidence and ability to do what is needed. Finishers rarely arrive in ideal situations, but their impact can often be match-defining."I feel very comfortable going out there on the day and any situation can arise which I really enjoy," Jacks said."It is not the same every day which you get opening so it keeps that fresh element to the game."At the beginning of my career it felt like you are just fighting to play in the next game, which is not the best place to be."It is a luxury to know, say when we go to Headingley [for the second ODI], that I will be in the team. You can't take that for granted and appreciate the hard work you have done to get there."It is also easy to forget Jacks began the year in England's Test side, as their spinning all-rounder during the Ashes - a role now filled by Dan Lawrence.Jacks, who met new Test coach Stephen Fleming when the New Zealander joined the white-ball squad at Old Trafford last weekend, has signed up for a stint with MI Cape Town in the SA20 this winter.There would no clash there with Fleming's first tour in charge in South Africa over Christmas, but the later part of the T20 competition overlaps with England's two Tests in Bangladesh, where English spinners will be needed."I don't know about what would happen or even if they would want me," he said."We will finish the summer before getting into the winter."For now, Jacks will focus on white-ball trips to Pakistan, Australia and South Africa as England build towards the 50-over World Cup next autumn. One downside of a Test recall would be losing more time to rearrange that Edinburgh trip."It didn't go how we planned but we will have to find time to redo it," Jacks smiled.

schema.headline: England vs Sri Lanka: Will Jacks explains the "scary" detail behind emergency appendix surgery

title: Man Utd still £1bn in debt, with interest costs rising and £63.5m spent on new stadium
description: In addition, United also confirmed they spent £63.5m of an additional $125 (£94.14m) added to their historic debt during a summer refinancing move on
body: In addition, United also confirmed they spent £63.5m of an additional $125 (£94.14m) added to their historic debt during a summer refinancing move on land for their new stadium. The club has not explained what it has done with the remainder. The stadium itself is likely to cost in excess of £2bn.It means the club's overall debt, while reducing from £1.3bn at the end of December, is still over £1bn, made up of the historic debt, which now stands at £577.6m, the £111.4m outstanding on its revolving credit facility, and outstanding transfer fees, which club sources say represents approximated 75% of the £473m listed and being owed as 'trade and other payables'.This comes at a time when supporters are furious about what they believe to be chronic under investment in Michael Carrick's first team squad this summer.United spent £148m on three new signings - Carlos Baleba, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans - this summer. It was less than a third of the £458m Manchester City invested in their squad and lower even than newly promoted Ipswich.However, fans are angry there was no additional left-back purchased to provide competition for Luke Shaw, who has missed three matches due to injury already, or striking support for Benjamin Sesko, who missed pre-season as he recovered from a shin complaint that has already resurfaced.While United argue the additional funds were earmarked for their stadium, to be built 350 yards away from where Old Trafford stands, the loan itself is lodged within club accounts."We are pleased to have secured record revenues," said chief executive Omar Berrada."This demonstrates the underlying strength of our business, and shows the direct impact of the work we have been doing over the past two years."While these results confirm that we are on the right trajectory, we will continue to take a disciplined approach to ensure our finances remain sustainable."With that financial sustainability in mind, we have strengthened both our men's and women's teams during the summer window and our men's team has seen the return of Champions League football to Old Trafford."United have also been criticised for a lack of investment in the Women's Super League squad, which is currently second bottom of the table with one point from three games.Ratcliffe previously argued the club had to take strong action to slash losses. Two lots of redundancies led to 450 people losing their jobs, while United have confirmed their latest set of salary costs have reduced by £11.3m to £302m."This is primarily due to changes in the make-up of the men's first team squad, combined with savings associated with headcount reduction programs implemented over the previous two fiscal years," said the club.

schema.headline: Man Utd still £1bn in debt, with interest costs rising and £63.5m spent on new stadium

title: Police looking at video of anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas slashing at boat with knife
description: Police are looking into a video appearing to show anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas slashing at an inflatable boat with a knife in the English Chann
body: Police are looking into a video appearing to show anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas slashing at an inflatable boat with a knife in the English Channel.The boat had been carrying about 50 migrants who had launched from a beach in Normandy. They were picked up by two RNLI lifeboats once they had reached the UK search and rescue area and were taken to Dover for processing.Daniel Thomas, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, had been filming the transfer from a yellow speedboat while giving commentary to a live stream audience of more than 15,000 people.The video then shows him sailing up to the boat, taking out a small knife and start slashing at the side of the migrant boat.There were no migrants on board, but there was a French official from the coastguard vessel Abeille Liberté.As the Frenchman boarded the empty migrant boat mid-Channel Thomas shouted "Right, you are on English territory. This is England. This is not France any more."Then he made a series of stabbing and slashing movements against the rubber side of the large inflatable boat."Get off - get off," he shouted. "You've got time to get off the boat."It was not clear from the live stream if he did any damage to the boat."We just wanted to make sure that boat was not taken back to France and used again," Thomas told his followers.Posting on X, campaign group Stand Up To Racism described the footage as "disgusting".

schema.headline: Police looking at video of anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas slashing at boat with knife

title: Nigella Lawson is 'brilliant addition' to The Great British Bake Off, TV critics say
description: Nigella Lawson is 'icing on the cake', TV critics say as she enters Bake Off tentImage source, PA MediaImage caption, Nigella has taken over from Prue
body: Nigella Lawson is 'icing on the cake', TV critics say as she enters Bake Off tentImage source, PA MediaImage caption, Nigella has taken over from Prue Leith as a judge on Bake Off, alongside Paul HollywoodBySteven McIntoshEntertainment reporter TV critics have described Nigella Lawson as the "icing on the cake" of The Great British Bake Off, after the show returned for a new series on Tuesday.Lawson has replaced Dame Prue Leith, who announced she was leaving earlier this year after nearly a decade in the programme's famous tent.The Telegraph said Lawson gives the Channel 4 series a "new lease of life", while Digital Spy agreed she was a "brilliant addition" to the line-up.But the Independent was cooler on the launch episode as a whole, saying the show "wastes Nigella's prodigious charms and misses a chance for a true revamp".The return of Bake Off saw Lawson join fellow judge Paul Hollywood, who has appeared on the programme since its launch in 2010, and presenters Alison Hammond and Noel Fielding. Former Bake Off winner Giuseppe Dell'Anno told BBC Radio 4's Today that Lawson "did produce a step change" to the show and was a "nice fit with the ethos of the programme"."She was doing her best by capturing the vibes of a cake, the feelings, what it makes you think of, which was very nicely balanced by Paul being very technical and scrutinising," he said."I think, however, that she will get better over time, because my gut feeling yesterday was that she was still in new territory."Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Some critics noted Lawson did not deliver as much innuendo as expected during her first episodeIn a five-star review, the Guardian's Lucy Mangan said, external Lawson "moves through Bake Off dispensing words of wisdom, generous praise and gentle criticism".She added that Lawson is "just as confident as Leith but a much quieter, more soothing presence that works perfectly with Alison Hammond's ebullience and Paul Hollywood's teacher-ish vibe".The Telegraph's Anita Singh also awarded, external five stars, remarking that "Bake Off and Nigella are a match made in heaven"."She brings glamour, intelligence and poise. And, of course, a hefty dollop of innuendo," Singh said."Lawson is supportive in her judging but not afraid to tell the bakers where they can improve. She gives helpful advice."The launch episode was described as "one of the most disastrous openers ever" by Metro's Adam Miller, external - but luckily he was only referring to the cakes."When Bake Off should be crumbling after 17 seasons, Nigella Lawson is making Channel 4's crown jewel fresher than ever," he said."It's clear to see she is the lifeline Bake Off needed to ensure it could easily have another decade or more in it yet."'Stale format'However, other critics said Channel 4 had missed an opportunity to revitalise the programme.Awarding two stars, the Independent's Nick Hilton said, external Lawson quickly "feels part of the fabric"."But this is also the problem," he continued. "The Bake Off format is very tired. The cakes wobble, the decorations melt, the bakers over-salt the batter, and everything remains the same."Nigella's arrival might have been an opportunity for a harder refresh. But instead of bending the format to suit Nigella, the new judge bends to the will of the programme."Image caption, Prue Leith announced she was leaving Bake Off earlier this yearHilton acknowledged that producers "might have done brilliantly to snag Nigella, and it will undoubtedly lead to an uptick in viewers". "But they've applied her prodigious charms too thinly, and even she – with her preference for all things 'sumptuous' – can't stop the feeling that the show has gone more than a little stale."Several critics noted that Lawson did not deliver as much innuendo as expected during her debut in the tent."Add Nigella – famous for her on-screen coquettish eyelash-fluttering and cheeky language choices – into the mix, and you'd imagine the sauciness gets dialled up to 11,"  said the Radio Times's Jane Rackham, external."Instead, she's cut back on the sauce. She makes well-informed and helpful comments about the amateur bakers' efforts."Digital Spy's Janet A Leigh agreed, external, noting: "As is the nature of Bake Off, there were many opportunities for Nigella to engage with the playful, flirtatious nature that has underpinned the show since its inception. Yet every opportunity was gently rebuffed."Instead, she said, Lawson "has a way of talking about food that celebrates it and expands the audience's understanding of flavours without seeming pretentious"."If episode one is just a flavour of what to expect from Nigella, then it is hugely encouraging. She cares deeply, steers wisely, and slots effortlessly into the close-knit team." Image source, PA MediaWhen Lawson was faced with innuendo-laden comments from contestants or co-stars, she often "wisely said nothing", noted the Daily Mail's Jan Moir., external"Ultimately this was a tremendous debut performance from the new mistress of meringue, showing a side of Nigella we have not seen before: quirky, commanding, funny – but also humane," she concluded.Ben Dowell of the Times observed, external: "Bake Off has always been one of TV's more beguiling offerings with a comforting romance about it. "It's not perfect. Hammond is ebullience and warmth personified but her co-presenter, the erstwhile Mighty Boosh comedian Fielding, still looks a bit lost, as if he has wandered in from the wrong set."But with Nigella the show is definitely in safe hands. Bake Off has found a new star."

schema.headline: Nigella Lawson is 'brilliant addition' to The Great British Bake Off, TV critics say

title: Dolly Parton's manager accuses nephew who announced her death of threats and intimidation
description: Dolly Parton's management company has accused her nephew of "threats, intimidation, and coercion", revealing a bitter battle over the late star's lega
body: Dolly Parton's management company has accused her nephew of "threats, intimidation, and coercion", revealing a bitter battle over the late star's legacy and business interests.The accusations against Bryan Seaver, who was Parton's head of security and was handpicked to announce her death last month, have been made public in US legal documents filed this week.The company that manages Parton's businesses and properties, She's Alive, is seeking a temporary civil restraining order against him.In court filings, She's Alive alleged that Seaver mounted "an obscene, deliberate and escalating campaign of threats", claiming he said he would ruin her empire if the estate did not pay him. He has denied the claims.In a statement to TMZ, external, he said that text messages and emails quoted in the court application had been taken out of context to make it look like he was threatening people."Nothing in this lawsuit were threats and most of the comments I stand by," he said."A lot of these messages are two guys having rage talk and crying on the phone together while we were grieving."Seaver, the son of Parton's sister Cassie, owns a company that provided the singer's  security detail for the last 20 years of her life.Last week, he was fired by She's Alive as head of security for her properties.In a statement at the time, Seaver and his company said the dismissal was "unexpected" and "unexplained".They added: "We refuse to be intimidated by those whose actions we believe are being taken in bad faith and with the intent to profit from the life of someone who willingly gave so much."The request for a restraining order was filed in Nashville on Tuesday by She's Alive, which is run by Parton's longtime manager Danny Nozell.The court documents quoted a series of exchanges in which someone, identified by the estate as Seaver, threatened to destroy Parton's brand.In one, he's alleged to have said he would become "the hand of retribution for my entire family", according to the court documents.Another said: "I'm going to set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly's brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It's going to be great. Or [expletive] pay me."The papers also claimed that Seaver used his experience as a military contractor to intimidate employees.In an exchange with one of Parton's lawyers, he allegedly described himself as a "killer" and said that on the day his aunt died, he had sold $27m (£20m) in arms and ammunition to the Haitian police."All I do is warfare... Everyone needs to be worried about what I might do," he was accused of saying, according to a copy of an email attached to the complaint.In his statement published on TMZ, Seaver said: "I am a career soldier and military contractor and do conduct arms deals for foreign governments. I am a security professional and I am a killer."But he denied making threats and said he had been "talking frankly in a private way with Danny who I thought was my friend".The messages have resulted in some employees and lawyers for Parton's trusts and estates resigning, according to the court documents.She's Alive has also had to hire private security for its employees, including at their homes, the filing states.The BBC has contacted Seaver and She's Alive for further comment.Previously, Seaver was known to the public for announcing his aunt's death in a video posted to her Instagram account on 25 August. Speaking in front of a black background, he was sombre and reflective as he introduced himself and shared the unexpected news. "This video announcement is something Dolly asked of me years ago, before I fully absorbed it as a future reality," he said in the video.Seaver added that he had followed in his father Larry's footsteps in becoming Parton's head of security, a post he held for more than 20 years.Nozell started working for Parton in 2004, first as a tour consultant and later as her manager.In the 2019 Netflix film, Dolly Parton: Here I Am, he said his job was to transform her from a "heritage act" into a "superstar", and he took responsibility for reviving her international touring career.In a statement last month, he said the singer had "worked up until the day she died" on multiple projects, and envisioned a legacy that continued long beyond her death."She loved seeing her dreams come to life, and loved knowing her work brought people joy," he said in the statement."Ever the planner, Dolly worked with the team that she handpicked, for the past several years to build a project roadmap that will guide us for decades to come."The estate now faces a public tug of war over that legacy.

schema.headline: Dolly Parton's manager accuses nephew who announced her death of threats and intimidation

title: UK warned over ballooning debt costs and slower growth ahead of Budget
description: The UK has been warned over ballooning debt costs and slower economic growth ahead of Chancellor John Healey's first Budget next month.The UK was amon
body: The UK has been warned over ballooning debt costs and slower economic growth ahead of Chancellor John Healey's first Budget next month.The UK was among countries facing downgraded growth forecasts in a report by the influential Organisation of Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) on Wednesday.That came as the head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) told the BBC that Britain and the US needed to reduce debt due to spiralling borrowing costs.The ongoing conflict in the Middle East and the Russia-Ukraine war has pushed up the cost of crude oil leading to higher fuel and energy costs, which in turn has driven up inflation around the world.The UK economy will grow by slightly less than expected next year, according to the OECD which now expects growth of 1% next year rather than 1.1%.However, it said the UK had proved more resilient than expected this year, upgrading its forecast for growth 0.9% to 1.1%.Meanwhile, IMF head Kristalina Georgieva told the BBC on Tuesday that global economic shocks had been "pushing debt levels up like a staircase not to heaven" but that governments had taken "no action to contain that service cost"."[It's] time to take that action," she said, adding that "courage" was needed by politicians to take the necessary steps.Inflation has also pushed up the cost of interest on government debt, which alongside an unexpected surge in government borrowing in August has added to the pressure on Healey.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday that the UK's high level of borrowing had left it "over-exposed" to global shocks.However, he said he stood by his point - made a year ago -  that Britain should be less "in hock" to investors in the bond markets. At the time, the comments spooked investors due to fears he was calling for spending restraints to be eased. Burnham has made easing the cost-of-living for households one of his key aims, while the government is under pressure to spend more on defence.He and Healey face a difficult balancing act, trying to offer more support to households while sticking to Labour's manifesto commitments on tax and the government's self-imposed fiscal rules. The impact of higher fuel prices next year depends on how long supply disruptions last, and stockpiles of oil and supplies from outside the Gulf states have helped cushion the effects on economies so far, the OECD said.Budget airline Ryanair will put up prices next summer as a result of persistently higher oil prices. Chief executive Michael O'Leary said ticket prices will be "materially higher", adding that carriers are in an "almost unprecedented" situation.Ryanair's fuel bill could jump by $1.5bn (£1.1bn) next year to $7.5bn, he said.Risks to the global economy include weaker-than-expected returns on AI investment and climate-change related supply shocks, the OECD said.Next year, global growth is expected to also be 0.1% lower, with countries affected including Australia, Canada, and the Euro-area.Weather-related shocks, including from a strong El Nino, could hit farmers and help push up food prices, it added.In addition, tariffs and export restrictions on trade continue to add to uncertainty, it said. New US tariffs from July as part of the Trump administration's ongoing volatile trade policy have raised its effective tariff rate by 1%.Chief Secretary to the Treasury Emma Reynolds said: "Despite unprecedented pressures and conflict in both the Middle East and in Europe, the UK economy is showing strong resilience."She added that the government is "already giving families space to breathe" and "starting the big, long-term changes needed to create good jobs and growth in every postcode".However, Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said the OECD urges countries to "control spending and improve public sector efficiency"."Instead, this government is trying to find new ways to tax you whilst having to pay interest rates on their borrowing which are the highest in the G7," he said.Ruth Gregory, deputy chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said that the UK had "so far remained resilient to higher energy prices", but most of that reflected businesses having built up stock and households not putting so much disposable income into savings.However, this effect would be temporary, with growth more muted next year.She added that the "drag" on the economy from energy prices would pick up, while as a percentage of the UK's economic output, debt interest payments are forecast to hit levels seen in the mid-1980s.

schema.headline: UK warned over ballooning debt costs and slower growth ahead of Budget

title: Football scouting: Hidden gems and the race to discover emerging talent
description: Hunting hidden gems - is there anywhere in the world left to scout?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Dario Osorio, 22, has won 25 caps for Chil
body: Hunting hidden gems - is there anywhere in the world left to scout?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Dario Osorio, 22, has won 25 caps for Chile and has featured twice for Crystal Palace since joining on loan this summerByAlex BysouthBBC Sport senior journalistThe world's biggest clubs were all aware of the teenage sensation turning heads for Universidad de Chile, the one dubbed his generation's Alexis Sanchez."When we signed Dario Osorio, it was not because no-one knew about him," Kristian Kjaer, technical director at Midtjylland, tells BBC Sport.Osorio was on the radar of AC Milan, RB Leipzig, Salzburg and a number of other English and German clubs before he left Santiago for Denmark at the age of 19.It was a carefully considered pathway. After three seasons in Scandinavia, the winger joined Crystal Palace on loan this summer with a £24m option to buy which would make him the most expensive sale in Danish Superliga history.Midtjylland, where Brentford owner Matthew Benham was a majority stakeholder between 2014 and 2023, are renowned as one of the most innovative clubs in Europe for their use of analytics - from set-pieces to smart recruitment."We work on both pathways," explains Kjaer. "We have subjective scouting, more classic video scouting, live scouting, a network, people we trust in the club and also our partners. And then we have the data scouting."And Dario Osorio, we were aware of him long before we signed him."From feet-on-the-ground to the increasing availability of footage, data analytics and artificial intelligence, Premier League clubs - whether buying direct from source or tracking players like Osorio's progress - have a large proportion of the world's emerging talent covered. "That hidden gem kind of thing almost does not exist any more in football," says Kjaer. "Sometimes it does, but it's rare."'Find me a player like Ashley Cole...'Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Malick Yalcouye began his career at ASEC Mimosas, joining Brighton from IFK Goteburg two years ago and breaking into the first team this season following loan spells at Sturm Graz and Swansea"You would put this period as one of the most transformational in talent ID and recruitment," explains Sam Turner, head of operations at scouting and development platform Eyeball.Clubs can now obtain an incredible level of detail on players across the globe before they have even made a senior appearance. Eyeball, for example, was founded five years ago to focus on those predominantly aged 13 to 21.It is used by more than 60% of clubs in Europe's top five leagues, and a majority of Premier League sides, for access to more than 400,000 young players across 42 global markets from Europe to Africa and Latin America.Winger Malick Yalcouye, a new 20-year-old star at Brighton, was tracked on the system since developing at Ivorian side ASEC Mimosas, likewise Bazoumana Toure, who is now at Newcastle.The breadth of coverage is highlighted by other recent moves - Josue Caicedo left Ecuador's LDU Quito for Barcelona, Mustapha Nyassi swapped Gambia's Real de Banjul for Copenhagen and Nour Ashraf joined Leipzig from Egypt's ENPPI."The availability of data and footage has prompted a change in methodology," says Turner. "That has brought a load of benefits in terms of data-led recruitment, time saving, cost saving."Eyeball takes north of 2,000 data points every match, typically from leading amateur clubs and elite academies who film and upload their fixtures.The result is a huge database allowing analysts to watch all of a player's progressive passes, for example, discover who covered the most distance or simply ask 'find me a player like Ashley Cole'."There is always this human feel that can never be lost," adds Turner. "I like to think we have aided scouts and recruitment teams, supplemented them with the tools, data, information to be able to make more informed decisions on a more consistent basis."Data, says Midtjylland's Kjaer, is "extremely important because it gives you an objective tool you can lean towards" when complemented by years of decision-making experience."We cannot just turn on the computer and it tell us who to sign and then we go sign them," he says. "We also need to know about the cultural background, the family background, to make sure they fit into our football club."Of course, data has given us opportunities. We sign young. So the sample size will simply be smaller for us because if we are waiting until it's big enough, Brighton and Liverpool and Brentford and other guys, they will sign the player in front of us."Where are the emerging markets?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Both Kjaer and Turner see Uzbekistan as one of the emerging talent markets, with 22-year-old Manchester City defender Abdukodir Khusanov among those to feature at the World Cup for the debutants this summer"We can find interesting players all around the world," explains Kjaer."I like us to be open-minded. We are particular in the way we play and the way we sell. And therefore, we need to find these players who fit that style of play."When you have done your due diligence and you feel certain, pull the trigger. The pace in decision-making is also a hidden gem."One country regularly mentioned is Uzbekistan, who played in their first World Cup this summer, while Turner says Azerbaijan is pioneering a national talent network and "very forward-thinking and motivated to progress the game domestically".Then there is Japan, which Turner calls a "guiding star" in youth development for a system which takes players from grassroots, to school and college football and then the professional game. Think Kaoru Mitoma's thesis on dribbling techniques.For European clubs, it makes identifying young Japanese prospects more complex.Latin America, too, remains a hotbed of talent.As former Midtjylland chairman Rasmus Ankersen, who has since worked for Brentford and Southampton, wrote in his book The Gold Mine Effect, a club such as Cruzeiro will reject 4,000 players under the age of 15 for every one they take in. Brazilian clubs are naturally protective of their assets."They know eventually players will leave," says Turner. "But it is allowing them to leave at the right age where those clubs can benefit locally. And we are very invested in that."Much of the region, however, remains "untapped" but recording games creates opportunities."It's just a visibility piece for a lot of these players that means they don't get picked up," says Turner."We have gone a long way in solving that for a lot of markets, but there are many more that can be picked up with brilliant players everywhere."One of those markets continues to be Africa.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Winger Zadok Yohanna, 19, recently made his debut for Brighton after a year in Sweden at AIK"There'll be thousands," says Thomas Randolph, founder of Delphlyx, when asked whether talented African players may have missed out on big moves in the past.Delphlyx works with Premier League clubs and ownership groups, and others across Europe, the United States and Mexico, to provide information on the best - and most relevant - 14 to 21-year-olds in West Africa, often through data, live scouting and private tournaments. "We have over 19,000 players in Africa on our platform that you could just sit right here in London and watch, then pick up the phone, call one of them and organise a trial or a transfer. That just wasn't happening before," adds Randolph. With a projected average age of just over 18, Randolph says the region is a "young, growing, developing space" - a "sporting mecca". Football remains the main passion, though NFL and NBA are starting to invest in certain countries.But Randolph disputes the idea African scouting is now saturated, citing a number of areas that remain relatively undiscovered, often because of conflict or logistics, with scouts drawn to the region's biggest cities."Zadok Yohanna is a good example," explains Randolph. "He moved to Brighton recently. He comes from Ikon Allah, which is a tiny and relatively unknown academy in northern Nigeria."The southern bit of Senegal is where Sadio Mane is from, where [Lamine] Camara is from, who Chelsea tried to sign, and there's only one team down there. So within all these big countries, there are certain regions that are less scouted."Historically, it was agents who brought players out of Africa rather than scouts discovering them, whereas Delphlyx aims to help clubs identify and analyse certain talent first so scouts can visit specific tournaments or showcases to watch targets.Randolph mentions eastern Mali, Togo, Guinea-Bissau and Burkina Faso but Benin, situated between Nigeria and Togo, is of particular interest for the way the country has invested federation grants in football infrastructure and pitches."One place they've used the Fifa money very well is Benin," says Randolph. "It's now produced probably a future female Ballon d'Or winner - Romaine Gandonou, who's 15, just played at the Under-20 World Cup, and got the likes of PSG, Barcelona, everyone after her."Benin is going to be a country that over the next few years will become very interesting."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Striker Romaine Gandonou, 15, has already scored for the Benin senior sideSome Premier League clubs are buying directly from Africa. At 18, Senegalese defender Mor Talla Ndiaye has already been on the bench for Liverpool after arriving from Amitie, owned by ex-Newcastle and Chelsea striker Demba Ba.Ndiaye was spotted at last year's Under-17 World Cup, where Burkina Faso midfielder Mohamed Zongo also impressed. He will join Chelsea and Strasbourg owners BlueCo's project when he turns 18 in two years' time."The Under-17 World Cup is a big one," says Randolph. "If your African nation plays there and you do well, you're going to get a good move."Scouts have also been at the recent Under-17 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying and Delphlyx has helped organise trials for players from Senegal and Gambia at Premier League clubs.The pool is narrowed, however, because players must obtain a Governing Body Endorsement to be granted a work permit or - most likely - take one of a club's four Elite Significant Contribution spots, which essentially comes down to how many youth or senior internationals they have played.It's part of the reason young players initially move to European countries where regulations are less stringent and why Randolph believes Scottish clubs, where the same criteria does not apply, should be looking into the African market the way Scandinavians do.Nordsjaelland are unique in that the Right to Dream academy - founded in Ghana in 1999 by former Manchester United scout Tom Vernon - bought the Danish club seven years ago to provide a pathway for its biggest prospects, which have included Mohammed Kudus, Simon Adingra and Kamaldeen Sulemana.Brighton's Yalcouye and Newcastle's Toure made their first moves to Swedish clubs IFK Goteborg and Hammarby, while Midtjylland have a partner club in Nigeria, FC Ebedei. Coventry's Frank Onyeka played for both on his way to the Premier League, as did Paul Onuachu, now at Trabzonspor.Like with Osorio, and others such as Guinea-Bissau forward Franculino, who left this summer for Trabzonspor, or Ivory Coast defender Ousmane Diomande, now at Nottingham Forest via Sporting, Midtjylland can highlight a track record of developing young players before selling them on."I see Midtjylland a bit like Silicon Valley for tech companies - we have produced so much talent over the years," explains Kjaer."We can focus only on the development. Of course, we need to win, but it's a bit more of a secure environment."What we say is, if you want to focus on your career as a football player, you have to come here because that is the only thing we do. That is what we are experts in."Undiscovered talent on the doorstep?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Riyad Mahrez was 19 when he joined a professional club for the first time with Le HarveThere remains, however, undiscovered talent close to home. France, particularly Paris, boasts an incredibly rich talent pool.A unique national youth league system, where amateur sides face professional academies - and regularly beat them - offers clubs the chance to witness unsigned prospects competing against the most gifted players in their age group."Scouts from all over the world come to Ile-de-France to look at players in our leagues," said Jamel Sandjak, president of the Ligue de Paris Ile-de-France, which boasts more than 1,000 clubs and 270,000 players."Most of the France national youth teams are full of our players. So our regional teams are playing at national level."Last season, amateur side ES Nanterre, from the outskirts of Paris, won Championnat National Group B ahead of Champions League outfits Lens and Lille and second-tier clubs Reims, Bastia and Red Star.Forward Exauce Luyindula was the division's top scorer for renowned amateurs AAS Sarcelles - where Riyad Mahrez played until he was 18 - and has since joined Ligue 2 Guingamp.Other Eyeball, external partners enjoyed memorable victories, too. AFC Creil beat Lens at under-15 level, Olympique Rovenain's under-19s beat Nice and CS Bretigny's under-17s edged Paris St-Germain."Until recently, the vast majority of clubs were relying on the fact the best players are in the best academies or national talent systems, when actually a lot of those players were chosen by 12 or 13," explains Turner."A lot of the time that can be right, but also statistically the best players at 12 aren't always the best players at 18."There is such a high concentration of players in that region, there is not enough space. The best players aren't necessarily in the national systems."

schema.headline: Football scouting: Hidden gems and the race to discover emerging talent
